name: Busy-CPU leak probe (throughput_bench.py --cpu-probe)
code: main at 8c0ad2d (after v0.10.2); the shaper's tick skipping is unchanged since the WF pilot

host.where: owner's laptop, user-namespace lab (unshare --map-auto), no network beyond veth

setup.load: 2 busy loops on the client's cores 0,1 (servers on 2,3), random balanced on/off schedule
setup.observed: the client's outgoing carrier packets at the first hop's ingress

findings: Catch-up off (today's default): loading the client's cores is visible on the wire in 3 of 3 runs, count AUC 0.93-1.00 (0.92-1.00 as recorded), p = 0.0005 each (the smallest the test gives); 2.2-4.1% fewer packets per loaded window. This reproduces locally the mechanism behind 81% k-FP on real sites (WF_REAL_PILOT.json).

Catch-up 50 ms: the count per window is restored (count AUC 0.43-0.51, p 0.31-0.85, not significant), but the spread of the gaps between packets still separates loaded windows almost perfectly (gap_sd AUC 0.001-0.068, i.e. wider gaps in nearly every loaded window; p = 0.0005 each): packets are sent late and bunched. This matches the pilot's ~50% k-FP with catch-up.
So a fix must remove both the count and the timing signal. The probe now scores both (count, gap_sd, max_gap) and is the regression gate for the fix.
caveats: The runs recorded counts only; timing was re-scored from the raw captures after the fact. The window start was not saved by that version, so it was recovered as the offset that reproduces the recorded counts (alignment_packet_error = packets that differ, out of about 190,000 per run). New runs save the start.
A synthetic CPU load, not a browser: it shows the mechanism, not a fingerprinting accuracy.
auc_convention: AUC = P(a loaded window's value is the smaller one). 0.5 is chance; the further from 0.5 in either direction, the better the schedule shows. Fewer packets under load gives AUC near 1 for the count; wider gaps under load give AUC near 0 for gap_sd and max_gap.
